title: Triangles of the neck
summary: One muscle divides the neck, and everything else is described from it.

steps.title: Sternocleidomastoid divides the neck
steps.text:
It runs from the manubrium and medial clavicle to the mastoid process and superior nuchal line. Everything in front of it is the anterior triangle, everything behind it the posterior triangle.

Acting alone it turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head to the same side; acting together the two flex the neck. It is supplied by the accessory nerve (XI), which then crosses the posterior triangle.

check.q: What are the attachments of sternocleidomastoid, and what does it do?
check.a: Manubrium and medial clavicle to the mastoid process; one side turns the head to the opposite side, both flex the neck.

steps.title: The carotid sheath
steps.text:
Deep to sternocleidomastoid lies the carotid sheath: common carotid artery medially, internal jugular vein laterally, vagus nerve between and behind. The ansa cervicalis is embedded in its anterior wall.

The common carotid divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage – C4, the level of the carotid sinus and body.

check.q: Name the three contents of the carotid sheath.
check.a: Common (then internal) carotid artery, internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve.

steps.title: The posterior triangle
steps.text:
Bounded by sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and the middle third of the clavicle. It contains the accessory nerve crossing from the upper third of sternocleidomastoid's posterior border to the lower third of trapezius – very superficial, and easily divided during lymph node biopsy, leaving a drooping shoulder and weak shrug.

Its floor carries the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus and the phrenic nerve on scalenus anterior.

check.q: A firm lump in the posterior triangle of an adult. What is the first thing you must exclude?
check.a: A malignant lymph node — from the head, neck or, for a supraclavicular node, the chest or abdomen.

steps.title: The thyroid gland
steps.text:
Two lobes and an isthmus over the second to fourth tracheal rings, wrapped in pretracheal fascia – which is why it moves on swallowing. The recurrent laryngeal nerve lies in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and the external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery; both are the classic casualties of thyroidectomy.

The microanatomy model of thyroid follicles shows what the parenchyma looks like.

check.q: Why does a thyroid swelling rise when the patient swallows?
check.a: Pretracheal fascia binds the gland to the larynx, which rises during a swallow.

steps.title: The anterior triangle has four rooms
steps.text:
The anterior triangle is bounded by the midline, the lower border of the mandible and the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The digastric and the superior belly of omohyoid subdivide it into smaller working regions.

The submental triangle lies between the anterior digastric bellies; the submandibular triangle lies below the mandible between the two digastric bellies. The carotid triangle lies between sternocleidomastoid, posterior digastric and superior omohyoid. The muscular triangle sits nearer the midline over the strap muscles and visceral structures. Find the large triangle first, then add its internal borders.

check.q: Which two muscles provide the main internal boundaries of the anterior triangle?
check.a: Digastric and the superior belly of omohyoid.

steps.title: A superficial nerve and a deeper plexus
steps.text:
In the posterior triangle, the accessory nerve crosses relatively superficially, deep to the investing fascia. The brachial plexus lies deeper, associated with the scalene muscles and the prevertebral fascial layer. They share a surface region but occupy different depths.

This distinction helps explain different weakness patterns. Accessory nerve injury affects trapezius and the shrug; a plexus injury can affect several movements and sensory territories in the arm. A triangle is a surface map, not a statement that all its contents lie in one flat layer.

check.q: Why does weakness of the shoulder shrug alone point to a different structure from widespread arm weakness after a posterior-triangle injury?
check.a: The shrug depends on accessory supply to trapezius, while broader arm functions travel through the deeper brachial plexus.

objectives: Divide the neck into anterior and posterior triangles
Name the subdivisions of each and their contents
Use the triangles to reason about a neck lump
Use the digastric and omohyoid muscles to subdivide the anterior triangle
takeaways: Sternocleidomastoid divides the neck; everything is described as in front of or behind it.
The carotid triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, the internal jugular vein and the vagus.
A lump in the posterior triangle is lymph node until proved otherwise.
The anterior triangle contains submental, submandibular, carotid and muscular subdivisions; the digastric and omohyoid provide key borders.

title: The orbit and eye movements
summary: Six muscles, three nerves, and how to work out which one is palsied.

steps.title: The bony orbit
steps.text: A four-sided pyramid whose thin medial wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid) and floor (maxilla) are the parts that blow out. The optic canal carries the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery; the superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI.

steps.title: The four recti
steps.text: All four arise from the common tendinous ring. Medial and lateral rectus purely adduct and abduct. Superior rectus elevates and inferior rectus depresses – but because the orbit points laterally and the muscles pull straight back, they do so best with the eye abducted.

check.q: Which nerve supplies the lateral rectus, and what happens when it fails?
check.a: The abducens (VI) — the eye cannot abduct and the patient has horizontal diplopia worse on looking that way.

steps.title: The two obliques
steps.text:
Superior oblique hooks through the trochlea and pulls the back of the globe up, so the eye looks down and in; it is the muscle you test by asking the adducted eye to look down. Inferior oblique does the opposite: it elevates the adducted eye.

LR6 SO4, all the rest 3. Lateral rectus is VI, superior oblique is IV, everything else is III.

check.q: What does superior oblique do when the eye is adducted?
check.a: It depresses it — which is how you test the trochlear nerve.

steps.title: The three palsies
steps.text:
III: eye down and out, ptosis, and – if the lesion is compressive, such as a posterior communicating aneurysm – a fixed dilated pupil, because the parasympathetic fibres run on the outside of the nerve.
IV: vertical diplopia worse on looking down and in; the head tilts away from the affected side.
VI: failure of abduction, convergent squint. Its long intracranial course makes it the first to go with raised intracranial pressure – a false localising sign.

check.q: A down-and-out eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil. Which nerve, and why does the pupil matter?
check.a: The oculomotor nerve (III). A dilated pupil suggests external compression, such as an aneurysm, rather than a medical palsy.

steps.title: The retina in section
steps.text: Behind all of this is the retina. Open the microanatomy model and follow the light: it passes through the whole neural retina before it reaches the photoreceptors, which face backwards towards the pigment epithelium.

steps.title: Look out for the recti, in for the obliques
steps.text:
The visual axis and the axis of the orbit are not parallel. As a result, superior and inferior rectus also have rotational and adducting components; the obliques have more than one action too. A muscle name alone does not tell you which eye position best exposes its vertical action.

With the eye abducted, upward and downward movement emphasise superior and inferior rectus. With the eye adducted, looking down emphasises superior oblique and looking up inferior oblique. This is the logic behind the H-shaped examination path. It changes the mechanical alignment before asking the muscle to act.

check.q: Which muscle is particularly assessed by asking an adducted eye to look down?
check.a: Superior oblique, supplied by IV.

objectives: Name the seven muscles in the orbit and their actions
Give the nerve supply of each and the rule that summarises it
Work out which muscle is palsied from the direction of diplopia
Use eye position to distinguish the vertical actions of rectus and oblique muscles
takeaways: LR6 SO4 — all the rest by 3.
Superior oblique depresses the adducted eye; inferior oblique elevates it.
A third nerve palsy gives a down-and-out eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil.
Vertical recti are assessed best with the eye abducted; the obliques are assessed best with it adducted.

title: The facial nerve
summary: Five branches, and how to tell Bell palsy from a stroke.

steps.title: Course
steps.text: VII leaves the pons, enters the internal acoustic meatus, takes a sharp turn at the geniculate ganglion, runs in the facial canal giving off greater petrosal, nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani, and emerges at the stylomastoid foramen.

check.q: Through which foramen does the facial nerve leave the skull?
check.a: The stylomastoid foramen.

steps.title: Through the parotid
steps.text: It then passes through the parotid gland – without supplying it – and divides into five branches: Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal mandibular, Cervical. Because the nerve splits the gland into superficial and deep parts, parotid surgery is really facial nerve surgery.

check.q: Name the five terminal branches of the facial nerve.
check.a: Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical.

steps.title: Upper versus lower motor neurone
steps.text:
The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, while control of the lower face is predominantly contralateral. A unilateral supranuclear lesion therefore often weakens the opposite lower face while relatively sparing forehead movement.

A lower motor neurone lesion of VII can weaken the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead. This includes a lesion of the facial nucleus or fascicle in the pons, as well as a peripheral nerve lesion. Forehead involvement alone does not exclude stroke; accompanying signs and the full pattern are needed to localise the lesion.

check.q: What motor pattern is suggested by weakness of both the forehead and lower face on the same side?
check.a: A lower motor neurone pattern affecting VII. The lesion may be in the pons or the peripheral nerve, so this finding alone does not establish Bell's palsy.

steps.title: Three branches tell you how far back to look
steps.text:
The greater petrosal nerve carries parasympathetic fibres towards the lacrimal and nasal glands. The nerve to stapedius supplies the small middle-ear muscle. The chorda tympani carries anterior tongue taste and parasympathetic fibres towards the submandibular and sublingual glands.

These branches leave while VII is still within the temporal bone. A sufficiently proximal lesion can combine facial weakness with reduced tearing, altered taste or hyperacusis. An injury limited to a terminal branch in the face cannot directly interrupt a branch that has already left the trunk farther upstream.

check.q: Why does altered taste accompanying facial weakness suggest looking proximal to the terminal facial branches?
check.a: Taste fibres leave through chorda tympani inside the temporal bone, before VII divides into its terminal motor branches.

steps.title: The nucleus is a lower motor neurone too
steps.text:
The familiar forehead comparison distinguishes a supranuclear pattern from a lower motor neurone pattern. It does not distinguish every stroke from every peripheral nerve disorder. A lesion of the facial nucleus or its fascicle within the pons can weaken the entire ipsilateral face.

Look for other findings to place that lower motor neurone pattern: eye-movement abnormalities or long-tract limb signs can indicate a brainstem location. Bilateral cortical input makes the upper face relatively resistant to a unilateral cortical lesion, but forehead movement is one clue in a pattern, not a standalone exclusion of stroke.

check.q: Can a lesion within the brain produce weakness of the whole ipsilateral face?
check.a: Yes. Damage to the facial nucleus or fascicle in the pons produces a lower motor neurone pattern.

objectives: Trace the facial nerve from the pons to the face
Name its five terminal branches and its branches within the temporal bone
Separate an upper from a lower motor neurone facial palsy
Use intratemporal branch functions to distinguish proximal VII injury from an extracranial branch injury
takeaways: Ten Zebras Bit My Cheek: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical.
Relative forehead sparing suggests a supranuclear pattern; whole-side weakness suggests a lower motor neurone pattern, which can arise in the pons or peripheral VII.
Branches given inside the temporal bone localise the lesion: hyperacusis, loss of taste, dry eye.
Greater petrosal, stapedius and chorda tympani branches leave before the stylomastoid foramen, so associated deficits can suggest a more proximal lesion.

title: The cerebral arterial circle
summary: How the circle is built and what each stroke territory takes out.

steps.title: Two supplies, one circle
steps.text: The brain is fed by two internal carotids in front and two vertebral arteries behind. The vertebrals fuse into the basilar, which divides into the posterior cerebrals. Posterior communicating arteries join those to the carotids, and an anterior communicating artery links the two anterior cerebrals – closing the circle.

steps.title: Anterior cerebral artery
steps.text: Runs forward over the corpus callosum and supplies the medial surface of the hemisphere. Its territory is the leg area of the motor and sensory homunculus, so occlusion gives contralateral weakness and sensory loss that is worse in the leg than the arm, often with a grasp reflex and urinary incontinence.

check.q: Which part of the body does an anterior cerebral artery stroke affect most?
check.a: The contralateral leg — its cortical territory is the medial surface of the hemisphere.

steps.title: Middle cerebral artery
steps.text:
The direct continuation of the internal carotid and the commonest site of embolic stroke. It supplies the lateral surface: face and arm motor and sensory cortex, and – on the dominant side – Broca's and Wernicke's areas.

Face and arm weakness worse than leg, with aphasia if dominant or neglect if not. Its lenticulostriate branches supply the internal capsule and are the vessels of hypertensive lacunar strokes and Charcot–Bouchard aneurysms.
focus: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2-segment)
Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery

check.q: Why does a middle cerebral artery stroke affect the face and arm more than the leg?
check.a: It supplies the lateral convexity, where the face and hand have the largest cortical representation.

steps.title: Posterior circulation
steps.text:
The posterior cerebral supplies the occipital lobe and inferior temporal lobe: occlusion gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, classically with macular sparing because the occipital pole also gets middle cerebral supply.

Branches of the basilar and vertebrals supply the brainstem and cerebellum, producing the crossed signs of lateral medullary and pontine syndromes.

check.q: Name three features of a posterior circulation stroke.
check.a: Vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia or visual field loss — any three.

steps.title: Berry aneurysms
steps.text:
The commonest sites are at branch points on the anterior part of the circle: the anterior communicating artery, the origin of the posterior communicating, and the middle cerebral bifurcation.

A posterior communicating aneurysm classically compresses the oculomotor nerve – a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil is a surgical emergency.

check.q: Where is the commonest site of a berry aneurysm?
check.a: The anterior communicating artery.

focus: Insular branches of middle cerebral artery (M2-segment)
Parietal branches of middle cerebral artery
steps.title: A surface ring cannot rescue every deep branch
steps.text:
Small perforating arteries leave the major cerebral vessels and enter the deep brain. Lenticulostriate branches from the middle cerebral artery supply parts of the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Other perforators arise from the anterior and posterior circulations.

The circle connects large arterial routes near their origins, but it does not create a parallel bypass around every tiny downstream branch. A small deep infarct can interrupt densely packed motor or sensory fibres and cause a substantial deficit. Distinguish the size of the damaged vessel from the importance of the tissue it supplies.

check.q: Why can a small perforator infarct cause marked weakness despite a patent cerebral arterial circle?
check.a: Deep perforators have limited collateral supply, and a small lesion can interrupt densely packed motor fibres in the internal capsule.

objectives: Name the vessels that form the cerebral arterial circle
Give the territory of each cerebral artery
Predict the deficit from an occlusion of each
Distinguish large communicating arteries from small deep perforating arteries
takeaways: Anterior cerebral: medial surface and the leg. Middle: lateral surface, face and arm. Posterior: occipital lobe.
Berry aneurysms form at branch points, most often on the anterior communicating artery.
The circle is anatomically complete in fewer than half of people.
The arterial circle can provide collateral routes between major trunks, but small deep perforators have much more limited alternative supply.

title: Ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid
summary: The route CSF takes, and where it gets blocked.

steps.title: The ventricular system
steps.text: Two lateral ventricles drain through the interventricular foramina of Monro into the third ventricle, then along the narrow cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and out through the median and lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space.

check.q: Which channel connects the lateral ventricle to the third?
check.a: The interventricular foramen (of Monro).

steps.title: Production and absorption
steps.text: About 500 mL a day is made by the choroid plexus, with a standing volume of roughly 150 mL – so it turns over three or four times a day. It is absorbed by arachnoid granulations into the superior sagittal sinus.

check.q: Where is cerebrospinal fluid produced and where is it absorbed?
check.a: Produced by the choroid plexus; absorbed through the arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses.

steps.title: Where it blocks
steps.text:
The aqueduct is the narrowest point, so aqueduct obstruction can produce non-communicating hydrocephalus with dilated lateral and third ventricles and a normal fourth. A posterior fossa lesion can instead obstruct the fourth ventricle or its outlets, producing a different pattern depending on the site.

Communicating hydrocephalus follows impaired absorption – after subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis – and dilates all four.

check.q: Which part of the ventricular system most often obstructs?
check.a: The cerebral aqueduct — the narrowest point.

steps.title: Put the blockage on the route
steps.text:
Imagine blocking one interventricular foramen: the lateral ventricle on that side is upstream and can enlarge. Move the blockage to the aqueduct, and both lateral ventricles plus the third are upstream, while the fourth is downstream.

Move it again to the outlets of the fourth ventricle, and the fourth can enlarge along with the ventricles above it. A posterior fossa lesion does not automatically produce one fixed pattern; the pattern depends on what it compresses. Trace the actual obstruction before naming the dilated spaces.

check.q: Which ventricle is downstream from an aqueduct obstruction but upstream from obstruction of the fourth-ventricle outlets?
check.a: The fourth ventricle.

steps.title: Fluid outside the ventricles still belongs to the route
steps.text:
CSF leaving the fourth ventricle enters the subarachnoid space, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord. Where that space widens around major contours it forms cisterns, rather than another set of internal ventricles.

The classic absorption route is through arachnoid granulations into dural venous sinuses; meningeal lymphatic and other outflow routes also contribute. Production, passage and removal must balance. A communicating ventricular system can still enlarge if CSF outflow is impaired after it has left the ventricles.

check.q: Why can hydrocephalus occur even when the aqueduct and ventricular outlets remain open?
check.a: CSF outflow or absorption can be impaired beyond the ventricular system.

objectives: Trace CSF from its production to its absorption
Name the four ventricles and the channels between them
Explain communicating and non-communicating hydrocephalus
Predict which ventricles enlarge from the precise position of a CSF obstruction
takeaways: Choroid plexus makes about 500 ml a day; the system holds about 150 ml.
Lateral → interventricular foramen → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → subarachnoid space.
The aqueduct is the narrowest point and the commonest site of obstruction.
An aqueduct obstruction enlarges the lateral and third ventricles upstream; obstruction of fourth-ventricle outlets can enlarge the fourth as well.

title: The spinal cord and its coverings
summary: Three membranes, two enlargements, and the tracts that explain the cord syndromes.

steps.title: Extent and enlargements
steps.text:
The cord runs from the foramen magnum to about L1/L2, ending as the conus medullaris and tethered by the filum terminale. Cervical (C4–T1) and lumbosacral (L2–S3) enlargements mark where the limb plexuses arise.

Because the cord is shorter than the canal, the roots below it run down as the cauda equina.

check.q: Where does the spinal cord end in an adult, and why is that not where the vertebral column ends?
check.a: At L1/L2 — the column grows faster than the cord after the third fetal month.

steps.title: The meninges
steps.text: Dura, arachnoid and pia, with the denticulate ligaments anchoring the cord laterally. The epidural space contains fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus – the route by which prostate and breast cancer reach the vertebrae – and is where an epidural is placed.

check.q: Which space does an epidural anaesthetic go into, and what does it contain?
check.a: The extradural space, containing fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus.

steps.title: Why the cord syndromes look the way they do
steps.text:
The dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception and cross in the medulla – so a cord lesion gives ipsilateral loss.
The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature and crosses within one or two segments – so a cord lesion gives contralateral loss, starting a couple of segments below.
The corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla – so a cord lesion gives ipsilateral weakness.

Put those three together and Brown-Séquard hemisection explains itself.

check.q: Why does a hemisection cause loss of pain on the opposite side but loss of vibration on the same side?
check.a: Spinothalamic fibres cross within a segment or two of entering the cord; dorsal column fibres do not cross until the medulla.

steps.title: A root and a ramus are not the same
steps.text:
A dorsal root brings sensory fibres into the cord, with their cell bodies in a dorsal root ganglion. A ventral root carries motor fibres out. They unite briefly as a mixed spinal nerve before dividing into dorsal and ventral rami.

Both rami now contain sensory and motor fibres. Dorsal rami supply the intrinsic back muscles and overlying skin; ventral rami supply the anterolateral trunk and limbs, forming plexuses where fibres are redistributed. The sensory-versus-motor distinction belongs to the roots, not to the two rami.

check.q: Is a dorsal ramus purely sensory because it has the word dorsal in its name?
check.a: No. Dorsal and ventral rami are both mixed; dorsal roots are sensory and ventral roots carry motor output.

steps.title: Blood supply explains another pattern
steps.text:
The anterior spinal artery, reinforced by segmental contributions, supplies much of the anterior two thirds of the cord. This includes anterior horn cells and important motor and pain-temperature pathways. The paired posterior spinal arteries contribute strongly to the dorsal columns.

An anterior cord infarct can therefore combine weakness with loss of pain and temperature while relatively preserving vibration and position sense. Real vascular territories overlap and injury varies, but the teaching pattern follows the same cross-sectional map you used for cord tracts.

check.q: Which sensory functions may be relatively preserved in a classic anterior cord syndrome?
check.a: Vibration and conscious position sense, because the dorsal columns have a different principal arterial supply.

objectives: Describe the extent of the cord and its enlargements
Name the main ascending and descending tracts and their positions
Explain why the cord ends at L1 and what that means for a lumbar puncture
Distinguish dorsal roots, ventral roots and mixed spinal nerve rami
takeaways: The cord ends at L1/L2; the dural sac continues to S2.
Cervical and lumbosacral enlargements supply the limbs.
Grey matter is central and butterfly-shaped; white matter is peripheral and arranged in tracts.
Dorsal roots carry sensory afferents and ventral roots motor efferents; after they unite, both dorsal and ventral rami are mixed nerves.
